A single shared window will always favor whichever category's season happens to fall into it, and the decision ends up made in favor of the calendar. In FMCG this mistake is especially costly, because the budget arrives at the season's peak, when the product is already selling well on its own, and by the next peak the money is already spent. The check is simple: before comparing two brands within one period, mentally shift the comparison to the opposite season. If the conclusion flips, you measured the calendar.

tasks.title: One brand's two distributions
tasks.brief: The "Nettora" brand manager shows numeric distribution falling from 82% to 33%; the director replies: "weighted is 47.5%, no need to panic". Both are right.
tasks.goal: Read the gap between the two measures.

tasks.predictQuestion: By June 2025 numeric lost 10.6 points and weighted only 5.1. What did that mean?

options.label: Small outlets were leaving: many addresses, little sales, the large ones are next
options.why: Weighted falls slower when the departing outlets are smaller than average. It is an early signal: by December weighted had already lost 34 points.

options.label: A calculation error: the measures cannot diverge so much
options.why: They can and must: numeric counts addresses, weighted the money behind them. They coincide only if all outlets are the same size, which no channel is.

hints: Weighted distribution is a share of turnover, numeric is a share of addresses. What has to be true about the departing outlets for many addresses to leave but little turnover?
Look not at the June gap but at what happened to both metrics by December.
tasks.explain: Numeric answers "in how many outlets is the brand", weighted "what share of trade do they make". Weighted is almost always higher: a brand is listed in large outlets first. Read the pair by the gap and how it changes: numeric falling faster than weighted means small outlets leaving; weighted catching up means the large ones are next.

tasks.title: Distribution at 94%, but the shelf is empty
tasks.brief: The sales report says "Aqualis" is in 94% of the chain's stores, yet the shelf audit found it missing 12% of the time. How are both figures right?
tasks.goal: Explain the gap between the two figures.

figure.note: Counted as distributed if at least one unit sold in the month: sales exist, so the store counts.

tasks.predictQuestion: Which conclusion is right?

options.label: Both are right but measure different things: the month and a moment
options.why: Sales-based distribution is a coarse sieve: one unit closes the month. A gap inside the month is invisible by construction, so availability is measured separately.

options.label: The audit is wrong: without stock the store would drop out
options.why: It would not drop out: the "one unit a month" rule survives a week without stock, or three. Sales did fall, but the metric does not show it.

options.label: Count distribution only if it sold every week
options.why: A threshold does not solve it: for a slow seller it gives false absence, and a gap inside the month stays invisible. Availability is measured by audit or stock.

options.label: The audit checked a sample, not all stores
options.why: A sample adds error but does not explain the gap. Even a full audit shows the same: it measures a moment, the report a month.

hints: Read the metric's definition literally: what's enough for an outlet to count in the month's distribution?
Ask yourself which event in the weekly table a sales report fundamentally can never see.
tasks.explain: Out-of-stock is a direct loss: the shopper came, found none and took another brand. Sales data cannot catch OOS in principle: sales record what happened, stock-outs are what did not. Measure availability separately, by shelf audit or stock.

tasks.title: Which distribution to bring back
tasks.brief: The decision is to put "Nettora" back on the shelf. The sales director sets a goal: 80% distribution. You ask which kind.
tasks.goal: Compare the cost of two wordings of one goal.

figure.title: Lost outlets, share of channel turnover
head: Outlets
Share of channel turnover
figure.note: Now (Q2 2026): 33 outlets of 94, numeric 35.1%, weighted 47.6%; 46 outlets lost. Winning back the first five: weighted 80.1%, numeric 40.4%. Numeric 80% means 43 of 46.

tasks.predictQuestion: What do you tell the director?

options.label: Reword it: weighted 80% is five negotiations, numeric 80% is forty-three
options.why: The same "80%" costs nine times different amounts of work. Until the goal says which distribution, sales and the analyst report on different things.

options.label: Win back five big outlets: numeric will follow
options.why: It will not follow: five outlets give numeric 40.4%, halfway. Starting with the big ones is sensible, but passing it off as achieving "80%" is a swap.

options.label: The goals are equal: 80% is 80%
options.why: The difference in how you count is the difference in work: money closes with five addresses, addresses need the whole list, including outlets worth 0.11% of turnover.

options.label: Win back all 46: there was demand there
options.why: The 16 smallest outlets together give under one percent of turnover. Spending as many negotiations on them as on the first four must be a conscious choice.

hints: Compute how many outlets are needed for each of the two goals. The numbers are in the setup.
Think about what happens a year from now if the goal stays worded as just "80% distribution".
tasks.explain: This task is not about distribution but about how a metric becomes a work plan. "Return distribution to 80%" sounds like one goal and unfolds into two projects: five negotiations with the big ones against forty-three visits, mostly to outlets worth hundredths of a percent of turnover. A goal always names the measure.

tasks.title: Wider doesn't mean bigger
tasks.brief: "Fruvia Apple" is in 52 outlets, Orange in 46, yet Orange sells a third more. Where does Apple's advantage go?
tasks.goal: Split volume into three factors.
tasks.predictQuestion: Where does Apple lose what it wins on distribution?

options.label: On both: it sells less often (33 weeks against 36.5) and less per week
options.why: Volume is a product of three factors, and leading on one guarantees nothing. Here the other two are lower, and the main drop is units per week.

options.label: Only on frequency: every fifth week it is missing
options.why: Frequency is lower, but the gap is 10%, against 25% in units per week. Naming a lesser lever sends sales to the wrong problem.

options.label: Nowhere: Apple has a lower price
options.why: Price would explain a revenue gap, but units are compared. The gap decomposes fully into frequency and weekly volume.

options.label: Not enough data: competitor sales are needed
options.why: You do not need competitors to decompose your own volume. They matter next: is 9.87 normal for the category?

hints: Compare the three factors one by one and compute the percentage difference for each.
Leading on one factor of a product says nothing about the product itself.
tasks.explain: In FMCG, market share is split into penetration, frequency and purchase size. We have no household panel, but the arithmetic is the same on outlet data: outlets × weeks with sales × units in such a week. The point is not the source but that leading on one factor guarantees nothing.

tasks.title: Everyone tried it, few came back
tasks.brief: A new snack flavor launched six months ago with a big ad campaign and free samples. The household panel shows penetration grew from 4% to 11%. Market share in money stayed unchanged. Marketing asks you to explain why.
tasks.goal: Determine which of market share's three factors failed to deliver.
tasks.scenario:
Household panel, before
launch and 6 months later:

  penetration
    (bought at least once)
    was 4%  →  now 11%
  purchases per buyer
    was 3.4  →  now 1.3
  average purchase size, ¥
    was 180  →  now 185

  market share in money
    was 2.1%  →  now 2.1%

Shelf space and price were
unchanged.
tasks.predictQuestion: What happened to the brand?

options.label: Lots of people were convinced to try it, and almost nobody came back: frequency fell from 3.4 to 1.3, and the penetration growth turned into one-off trial purchases
options.why: Penetration grew 2.75x, frequency fell 2.6x; the product stayed put. That's the signature of trial with no follow-up repeat purchase: the product got noticed, not loved.

options.label: Share didn't grow because the whole market grew: the brand grew along with the category
options.why: That would show up as steady frequency alongside growing penetration. Here frequency collapsed almost threefold; that's an event internal to the brand, not the market moving.

options.label: A panel error: penetration and market share can't move in opposite directions
options.why: They absolutely can; they're linked through the other two factors. Market share = penetration × frequency × purchase volume, and a drop in any one factor cancels out growth in the others.

options.label: The samples distorted the data: they were free, so penetration was computed off giveaways
options.why: The panel records purchases, not gifts, and the growth to 11% is people who paid. The problem isn't that the purchase wasn't real; it's that it stayed the only one.

hints: Multiply the three numbers before and after. What would have had to happen to the product if only one factor had dropped?
Ask yourself what separates someone who bought the product once from someone who bought it four times.
tasks.explain:
Market share in a consumer panel decomposes into three factors: penetration (what share of households bought the brand at least once), frequency (how many times those buyers repurchased), and average purchase size. Growth in any one factor guarantees nothing; what matters is the product.

The picture "penetration up, frequency down, share flat" is the most common and most expensive one in launches. It means the ad and sampling budget worked right up to the register: people tried the product, and it didn't live up to expectations. Repeat purchase is the only honest test of a product, and its absence can't be fixed with another ad wave. A second wave will just repeat the same cycle and bring the same people to one purchase again.

Hence the practical rule: a launch is judged not by penetration but by the repeat rate among triers and the time to a second purchase. Penetration shows whether marketing worked; repeat purchase shows whether the product worked. The first grows from money, the second only from the product, and confusing them means funding a failure for another quarter.

What to tell marketing: the campaign did its job, the next question isn't for them. Before planning a second wave, it's worth understanding why people didn't come back: taste, price per gram, pack size, shelf placement.

tasks.title: Speed off the shelf
tasks.brief: A chain's category manager is reviewing the range: a SKU that takes shelf and sells slower than the rest frees the space. The "Aqualis" portfolio, 12 months.
tasks.goal: Find the vulnerable SKU.
tasks.predictQuestion: Which SKU will the chain question first, and why?

options.label: Sport 0.75 L: shelves like the leaders, but sells two to three times slower
options.why: The chain pays for shelf. Sport is in 46 outlets, like Sparkling 0.5 L, but gives 4.48 units a week against 8.73: the worst return on the same space.

options.label: Still 5 L: the narrowest distribution, 40 outlets
options.why: Narrow distribution is our problem, not the chain's: in its 40 outlets it sells at 8.80, above the portfolio average. The manager cares about shelf return.

options.label: Sparkling 1.5 L: lowest among the 1.5 L
options.why: It loses to still 1.5 L, but 6.97 units is mid-portfolio, and it earns its space.

options.label: None: all sell, all volumes are positive
options.why: A range review is not culling zeros but ranking. A SKU goes when another sells faster from the same space.

hints: Compare volume per outlet, not total volume. The chain is deciding about its own store, not the whole country.
Find the SKU that has distribution like the leaders but a rate of sale like the laggard.
tasks.explain: Rate of sale is the measure a store judges your product by. Volume is distribution times speed: you build distribution yourself, speed decides whether you may keep it. Wide distribution with low speed is the dangerous mix: the chain will give those shelves to faster sellers.

The average brand-wide growth is an average over both those the promo touched and those it didn't.

It ran in chains, which are a quarter of brand volume, so the brand result and the promo result differ 3.5 times and both are arithmetically right. tasks.title: TRx grows, NRx falls

options.why: TRx is the accumulated base, NRx its replenishment. With a three to six month course, a fall in NRx reaches TRx with that lag. The TRx growth is inertia.

Imagine NRx dropping to zero tomorrow. What happens to TRx, and after how many months?

tasks.title: A market share that swings by half
tasks.brief: At an OTC portfolio review, the manager shows a slide: «Vitanor» share was 11% in March 2024, 49.5% in February 2025. The slide's conclusion: "share is unstable, we need an urgent retention program." You recomputed the same share over a rolling year.
tasks.goal: Choose the base to compute market share over, and explain why the monthly figure is misleading.
tasks.predictQuestion: Which conclusion is correct?

options.label: Share is stable and slowly declining: the monthly swings come from seasonality and competitor promos, the rolling year averages them out and shows −3 points over a year and a half
options.why: Vitamins and cold remedies peak in different months, so monthly share reflects the calendar, not brand positioning. In MAT, every one of the four brands' seasons enters the window in full, and what's left is what's actually happening: a slow loss of about three points.

options.label: Share really is unstable: the rolling year is just hiding the real swings under averaging
options.why: Averaging is exactly the point here. The swings are real as sales facts, but they repeat every year and aren't a change in brand position; that's precisely what needs to be separated out before launching a retention program.

options.label: Both series are useless: share in packs doesn't reflect market position, share in money is needed
options.why: Share in money is a different, also useful metric, but that's not the slide's problem. Share in yen, computed monthly, would swing just as much, for the same reason.

options.label: The drop from 49.5% to 24.4% is the key fact, and MAT is smoothing it away
options.why: That's comparing February to June, vitamin season against off-season. A drop like that repeats every year and will return by next February; it says nothing about the brand's position.

hints: Look at which months the brand peaks in. What do February, November, and January have in common for vitamins?
A rolling year is a sum over 12 months, shifted monthly. What always falls into it regardless of where you start?
tasks.explain:
Market share is a ratio, and in any single month both the numerator and the denominator swing. In an OTC portfolio, the brands' seasons don't line up: vitamins get bought in autumn and winter, cold remedies in December and March. In a month when a competitor's season peaks, your share drops even though you didn't lose a single pack. That's exactly what produces a swing from 11% to 49.5% sitting on top of a calm underlying picture.

MAT (moving annual total) is the sum of the trailing twelve months, shifted forward by one month at a time. A window like that captures every brand's season exactly once, no matter where you're standing, so the calendar drops out of the metric entirely. What's left is what share was meant to measure in the first place: 29.4% in March 2025, 26.1% in June 2026, down three points over fifteen months, a steady, slow decline.

The price paid for MAT is speed. A sharp event (a competitor launch, losing a pharmacy chain) gets smeared across twelve months and only becomes visible with a lag. That's why pharma typically watches a pair of series together: MAT for position, monthly for events, but conclusions about share are drawn from the first.

And a practical rule for any industry: for a ratio metric, always check the denominator separately. Before explaining a share drop by your own actions, check whether the market itself simply grew. Half the "we're losing share" slides are really telling a story about someone else's season.

tasks.title: Three numbers about one drug
tasks.brief: At a drug review meeting, three departments cited three different numbers for the same month. Nobody made a mistake. The manager asks you which one to put in the report for the board.
tasks.goal: Compare three data sources and pick the right one for the question.
tasks.scenario:
One drug, one month:

  shipments to distributors
    41,200 packs
    accounting system
  pharmacy sales to buyers
    36,800 packs
    panel, an estimate
  physician prescriptions
    29,400 prescriptions
    Rx panel, an estimate

Board's question: "is the
drug growing"
tasks.predictQuestion: What should you tell the manager?

options.label: All three numbers are needed, but they answer different questions: shipments say what we sold, pharmacy sales say what the patient bought, prescriptions say what the doctor decided. For the growth question, prescriptions and pharmacy sales come first, shipments third
options.why: Shipments are driven by our own sales department and the distributor's warehouse; they rise and fall for reasons unrelated to demand. Demand shows up in pharmacy sales, and its source shows up in prescriptions, and prescriptions turn before anything else.

options.label: Shipments: it's the only figure from the accounting system, the other two are sample-based estimates
options.why: A source's precision doesn't make it the right fit. Shipments are measured exactly, but they measure product movement toward the distributor, not demand: a quarter with stock-up buying will show confident growth even as actual consumption falls.

options.label: Pharmacy sales: that's final consumption, the other two numbers are redundant
options.why: Pharmacy sales are the single best metric, but prescriptions shouldn't be dropped: they turn earlier and explain why pharmacy sales will move a quarter from now. And shipments are needed to catch channel overstocking.

options.label: None of them: the numbers don't reconcile with each other, the discrepancy needs fixing first
options.why: The discrepancy here isn't a defect, it's how the chain is built: warehouses and time sit between a shipment, a purchase, and a prescription, and some prescriptions never even reach a pharmacy. Demanding they match means demanding the impossible and stalling the work.

hints: For each number, ask: whose decision does it measure: ours, the pharmacy's, or the doctor's?
Which of the three will move first if the drug starts losing the market?
tasks.explain:
In pharma, the same movement of product gets measured at three points, and those points belong to three different decision-makers. Shipments are a decision by our own sales department and the distributor's buyer. Pharmacy sales are the patient's decision at the counter. Prescriptions are the doctor's decision, made before any of the rest.

So the series don't match, and shouldn't. Two warehouses sit between a shipment and a pharmacy sale, which can make our quarter look great purely off stock moved into the channel. A patient sits between a prescription and a purchase: some prescriptions never reach a pharmacy at all, some get filled later, some get swapped for a different drug at the counter. The gap between 29,400 prescriptions and 36,800 packs isn't a signal by itself; one course of treatment takes more than one pack.

What to pick for "is the drug growing": watch pharmacy sales as the fact of demand and prescriptions as its leading indicator, and keep shipments alongside; they catch overstocking that's invisible anywhere else. The one-sentence answer for the board: demand is described by pharmacy sales, our shipments describe our own channel management, and the two shouldn't be confused.

And a discipline that saves hours: any report with a number in it needs a source and an event stated right next to it. Not "sales: 41,200", but "shipments to distributors, accounting system". A meeting where three departments cite three unlabeled numbers always ends in an argument about who's wrong, even though nobody is.

tasks.title: Sales down by half, the average outlet sells more
tasks.brief: «Nettora» revenue in Q2 2026 is half of the same quarter in 2024. Meanwhile the average outlet sells more than it did two years ago. The category manager asks for one sentence about what happened.
tasks.goal: Break the revenue drop into two factors and name the source.
tasks.predictQuestion: What happened to the brand?

options.label: The brand lost 46 of its 79 outlets, and that's the sole source of the drop: in the outlets that remain, it sells even better than before, and price is nearly unchanged
options.why: Revenue decomposes into outlet count and revenue per outlet, and the two factors moved in opposite directions: −58% and +22%. Their product reproduces the observed −49% exactly, so there's no third factor to look for.

options.label: Demand for the brand fell: people started buying household chemicals less often, which halved revenue
options.why: A demand drop would look like falling revenue per outlet. It rose 22%; wherever the brand is still stocked, it sells no worse, in fact better, than before.

options.label: There are two causes: both the lost outlets and a 3% price drop
options.why: The price really did drop, but three percent against a 49% overall decline is noise. Placing it beside a 58% loss of outlets means treating the main cause and a negligible one as equals.

options.label: There's not enough data: without a channel breakdown, it's impossible to say what happened
options.why: A channel breakdown is useful for the next step, figuring out exactly which outlets left. But the source of the drop is already unambiguously identified: two factors multiply to reproduce the observed result.

hints: Revenue = outlet count × revenue per outlet. See what happened to each factor.
Multiply the factors' relative changes together and compare against the change in revenue.
tasks.explain:
Decomposition starts by choosing an identity, an equality that's always true, not approximately. Here it's "revenue = outlet count × revenue per outlet." The identity guarantees the factors explain the change fully, with nothing left over for "other factors."

The check is mandatory and takes one line: 33/79 × 32,699/26,857 = 0.418 × 1.218 = 0.51, and revenue came in at 51% of the 2024 level. It reconciles, so the breakdown is correct and there's nothing more to look for. If it hadn't reconciled, the wrong identity was chosen, or the periods were computed on mismatched filters.

The conclusion for the manager fits in one sentence, as requested: the brand didn't lose demand, it lost shelf space, 46 of 79 outlets, and that's the sole cause of the drop. That conclusion immediately points to who should hear it: the conversation belongs with sales and chain buyers, not marketing or pricing. If revenue per outlet had been falling with outlet count unchanged, the recipient would be exactly the opposite.

That's the whole point of decomposition: it doesn't explain the cause, but it narrows the search down to one factor and hands the question to whoever can actually influence it. "Revenue fell 49%" isn't a task, because it has no owner. "We're no longer in 46 outlets" is a task with an owner, a deadline, and an obvious first step.

One more thing worth noting about the growth in revenue per outlet. It looks like good news, but deserves a separate check: some of it might not be the remaining outlets selling better, but the smallest outlets dropping out and lifting the average. That's a separate step to work through, and it needs to happen before "+22% per outlet" makes it into a deck as an achievement.

tasks.explain: A group average changes for two reasons: the members changed or the group's composition changed. The second is the mix effect, and it draws growth where there is none. Here it gives more than real growth: the departed averaged 24,738 ¥, those who stayed 29,810 ¥, and their exit lifts the average by 11%. Compare comparable outlets.

tasks.title: How far to take the analysis
tasks.brief: Analysis of the "Nettora" decline: revenue −49% = outlets −58% × revenue per outlet +22%. The director asks you to continue; a day and a half to the board.
tasks.goal: Choose the depth of analysis.
tasks.predictQuestion: Where do you continue?

options.label: A: split −58% by channel and chain: who left
options.why: A decomposition goes down to the link someone can influence. "There are fewer outlets" is an observation; "we left these chains" is a named person's task with a first action.

options.label: D: compare with the household chemicals category
options.why: The comparison with the market is needed but nearly closed: revenue per outlet rose, so demand where the brand stayed is intact. A falling category would show the opposite.

options.label: B: split +22% into growth and mix effect
options.why: It must be checked, half an hour, but it protects the wording, not the next step. The board's main question is what to do about the lost outlets.

options.label: C: split revenue per outlet into units and price
options.why: Depth is no value in itself: units and price explain revenue inside an outlet, and the drop is not inside, there it is growth. Precise but off the question.

hints: For each option, ask: who in the company gets a task from its result?
The analysis is finished not when the explanation looks elegant, but when it's clear who to hand it to.
tasks.explain: Decomposition easily becomes endless: any factor splits further, and each level looks more thorough. There is one stop sign: a link with an owner, a person or team who can influence it. Here it is the specific departed outlets and chains: a list of 46 addresses turns the analysis into a work plan.

tasks.title: What to do with each cell
tasks.brief: The ABC-XYZ matrix is built, nine cells are filled in. The logistics director asks for one rule per cell: where to hold stock, where not to, and what to do with the borderline items.
tasks.goal: Tie each cell of the matrix to a specific action.

tasks.predictQuestion: What allocation of effort is correct?

options.label: AX: precise stock calculation and auto-ordering, since a mistake here is the costliest; AZ: the main target for manual attention and safety stock; CX: a simple replenishment rule with no human involved; CZ: a candidate for order-to-demand or delisting
options.why: Attention is allocated by the product of a mistake's cost and its likelihood. AX is expensive but predictable, so it gets automated. AZ is expensive and unpredictable; it's the one cell where manual work actually pays off.

options.label: All attention on group A as a whole, group C ordered on a leftover basis
options.why: Half right: A really does matter more by money. But within A, AX and AZ need opposite treatment; the first can be trusted to auto-order, the second can't, and that's exactly the distinction XYZ provides.

options.label: Safety stock across every X item: demand is steady there, so shortages are unacceptable
options.why: The opposite: steady demand is exactly what lets you get by with a minimal buffer, because it forecasts well. Safety stock is the price of uncertainty, and it belongs where uncertainty actually is.

options.label: Delist the group C items: they contribute little revenue and take up warehouse space
options.why: A mechanical delist based on one cell is a common and expensive mistake. An item can be small in revenue and still necessary: it's what draws people into the store, it fills out a lineup a chain requires, or it holds the brand's shelf presence.

hints: For each cell, ask two things: how much does a mistake cost, and how likely is it?
Safety stock is needed where demand is unpredictable, not where it's large.
tasks.explain:
The point of the matrix isn't classification, it's that each cell calls for its own action. ABC answers how much a mistake costs; XYZ answers how likely it is. Multiply them and you get an allocation of attention: where a person is needed, where a rule suffices, and where it's worth dropping the item entirely.

AX (money with predictable demand): an ideal candidate for automatic ordering. The math is worked out once, then the system runs itself, and the freed-up attention goes where it's actually needed. AZ is the cell the whole matrix exists for: the mistake is expensive and likely, no formula will save you, it needs a person, a bigger buffer, and syncing with the promo calendar. CX (small stuff with steady demand): a simple replenishment rule, minimal involvement. CZ (small stuff that also swings): order to demand, minimal stock, and if problems are persistent, a question about delisting.

The main caveat is about delisting group C items. The matrix is built on one metric and knows nothing about an item's role in the assortment. A kids' yogurt might contribute a small percent of revenue and still be the reason a family picks your brand over the one next to it; a flavor lineup might be a condition of a chain contract. The delisting decision gets made after a conversation with the category manager, not off a matrix cell.

The second caveat is about recomputing. The matrix is a snapshot for a period, and an item moves between cells: a new product starts in C, a seasonal item shifts XYZ groups depending on the calculation window, and a declining brand slides into C while staying important. It's worth recomputing quarterly, and watching the transitions matters as much as the current position: a move from AX to BZ is a signal by itself, before it even shows up in revenue.
