options.label: The first row: before and after is the proof
options.why: Before and after cannot separate the promo from late summer, back to school and a competitor's moves. That is why three more rows are needed.

options.label: Other brands' 17% fall is cannibalisation: no real growth
options.why: Cannibalisation must be checked separately and in comparable categories: snacks and water compete weakly. It does not cancel growth: Krosti rose by 3,354 units.

options.label: Nothing: causation cannot be proven without an experiment
options.why: An experiment is stronger, but "experiment or no conclusions" means no conclusions. A control group is a working approximation and the trade-marketing standard.

hints: Ask what should have gone up if the cause were the season or a general market lift rather than the promo.
The three lower rows share one property, which one?
tasks.explain: Proof of an effect rests not on what happened but on comparison with what would have happened without the intervention. You cannot observe that directly, so you use a control group: those who lived through the same period without exposure. Here the control is double: on one axis the brand is fixed and the channel changes, on the other the channel is fixed and the brand changes.

tasks.title: The first paragraph of the email
tasks.brief: The "Nettora" decline analysis is done. The email goes to a director who reads on a phone.
tasks.goal: Choose the first paragraph.
tasks.scenario:
A  Attached is the "Nettora"
   decline analysis, with extract
   and method.

B  Revenue 1,079,055 ¥ versus
   2,121,702 ¥. Outlets 33 versus
   79.

C  "Nettora" lost half its revenue
   by leaving 46 of 79 outlets.
   Start with the five largest; I
   need your budget decision.

D  The situation is alarming:
   rethink the whole brand
   approach urgently.
tasks.predictQuestion: Which paragraph is right?

options.label: C: conclusion, support, decision request
options.why: The answer is in the first sentence, the numbers are picked for the conclusion, and it ends with what is needed from the reader. They can decide without opening the attachment.

options.label: B: facts only
options.why: Drawing the conclusion is your job. Without it you hand the task back to someone with no time or calculation context.

options.label: A: cover note, content attached
options.why: The reader learns only that work was done. People open an attachment only if the first lines made them.

options.label: D: decisive conclusion, no support
options.why: The conclusion does not follow from the analysis: the data is about shelf, the proposal about packaging and price. Confidence does not replace a link to facts.

hints: Read only the first two lines of each version. That's exactly what the recipient will see. After which one can he decide anything?
Check each version for three things: a conclusion, a number supporting it, and what's required from the reader.
tasks.explain: The conclusion goes first, before explanations and numbers: you went from data to conclusion, the reader goes the other way. Paragraph structure: conclusion, support, proposal, request. B is a virtuous-looking mistake: shifting the work. D is a conclusion with no tie to the data. The rest lives below and in the attachment.

tasks.title: One conclusion, three audiences
tasks.brief: The same «Nettora» analysis has to be told to three people: the CEO at a fifteen-minute committee, the head of the field team, and a fellow analyst who will maintain the report.
tasks.goal: Understand what changes in the delivery from audience to audience, and what never changes.
tasks.scenario:
One and the same fact: the brand lost
46 outlets out of 79, revenue in the
ones that remain grew 22%, and brand
revenue is down 49%.

Three recipients:

  CEO
    decides where the company's
    money goes
  head of the field team
    decides who negotiates
    with whom
  fellow analyst
    will maintain this report
    after you
tasks.predictQuestion: What should change from audience to audience?

options.label: Depth and emphasis: matched to the decision that person makes; the facts and numbers themselves never change
options.why: The CEO needs the scale of the problem and what it's worth; the field lead needs the list of outlets and the order to work them; the analyst needs methodology, filters and the limits of the data. It's one and the same conclusion, cut three ways for three different decisions, not three versions of the truth.

options.label: Only the length changes: shorter for the CEO, longer for the analyst, in between for the field lead
options.why: Length is a consequence, not a decision. The short version for the CEO differs from the short version for the field team not in size but in which fact made it in: what the issue is worth versus which outlets to visit.

options.label: The field team needs it simpler and without numbers: people in the field don't work with analytics every day
options.why: That swaps "for a different decision" for "for less clever people." The field lead needs the most concrete numbers of all, which outlets, in what order, whom to talk to; simplifying them makes the analysis useless exactly where someone will act on it.

options.label: Nothing: all three get the same document, otherwise you end up with three versions of the truth
options.why: A single version of the truth is about numbers and definitions, not about format. One document for everyone means it was written for nobody's decision, and each of them has to hunt for their part in it, and usually doesn't find it.

hints: Ask of each one: what decision will he make tomorrow morning, and which number does he need for it?
One of the options confuses "a different decision" with "simpler, for people who don't get it."
tasks.explain:
Delivery is determined not by the recipient's job title but by the decision they make. That's the only criterion that works: it tells you what to include, in what order, and where to stop.

The CEO needs the scale and the price: half the brand's revenue, a single cause, is it worth investing in a comeback or is closing the line more sensible. He doesn't need the list of outlets; he isn't going to visit them. The head of the field team needs exactly the reverse: which outlets, in what order, which chain is the key one, what to say to the buyer. For him the scale of the problem is one line of context. The fellow analyst needs a third thing: how it was computed, which filters, what counted as an outlet, where the data are unreliable, because his decision is "can this report be trusted, and how do I fix it."

What can't change for any audience are the facts, the numbers, and the caveats that bear on the conclusion. If the analysis has a weak spot (say, some outlets may simply have changed owner rather than dropped the brand), it travels into all three versions, because it changes the conclusion for all three. A caveat you dropped "so as not to overcomplicate things for the CEO" isn't simplification, it's distortion.

A separate word on the temptation to simplify for the field team. It looks like consideration and works like disrespect, and it damages the work: these are precisely the people who need the most concrete data, because they're the ones who will act. The difference between versions isn't in complexity, it's in which slice you put up front.

A practical technique: before writing, finish this sentence on the recipient's behalf, "having read this, I will…". If the sentence doesn't end in an action, the document isn't ready; either you haven't found which decision it serves, or this person doesn't need it at all.

tasks.title: A conclusion you're not sure of
tasks.brief: The analysis is due today. The conclusion is confirmed, but some of the 46 outlets may have closed. Checking takes a week.
tasks.goal: Pick wording that neither lies nor blocks.
tasks.scenario:
A  Say nothing: the conclusion
   holds and a caveat only
   confuses.

B  "The brand may have lost
   distribution, but this needs
   checking, no conclusions yet."

C  "46 of 79 outlets left the
   shelf, confirmed by sales. Some
   may have closed; I will check
   by the 12th. The conclusion is
   unaffected, the outlet list
   is."

D  Hand it over in a week, once
   checked.
tasks.predictQuestion: Which option is right?

options.label: C: confirmed, doubtful, impact, deadline
options.why: Three levels of confidence are named, plus what the uncertainty affects. The budget can be decided today, the outlet list after the 12th.

options.label: B: admit uncertainty, no conclusion
options.why: "May" without saying what is in doubt and how much reads as "the analyst is unsure of everything". The reader decides blind or not at all.

options.label: A: say nothing
options.why: The caveat will surface and trust in everything you bring suffers. Silence stops the reader from weighing the risk in their decision.

options.label: D: hand it over in a week
options.why: The confirmed part is enough for the main decision, and a week of idleness costs negotiations. Completeness bought with delay is also a mistake.

hints: Ask not "how sure am I" but "what exactly changes in the decision if this part turns out to be wrong."
One of the options is honest in form but gives the reader nothing to work with.
tasks.explain: Uncertainty is no reason to stay silent or to blur the conclusion: localise it. Three levels, explicitly: what is confirmed (sales stopped in 46 outlets), what is in doubt (the reason), what it affects and when you will know. Then the reader decides today what can be decided.

tasks.title: Four questions, four forms
tasks.brief: Four slides are going into the «Nettora» deck. The designer suggests making all the charts identical, "for a consistent look." You need to decide which form answers each question.
tasks.goal: Match each question to the chart form that answers it.
tasks.scenario:
Four questions in the deck:

  1  How did the brand's revenue move
     week by week over two years?
  2  Which five regions lost the most?
  3  Is an outlet's size related to
     whether it dropped the brand?
  4  What makes up the −49%: how much
     came from losing outlets, how much
     from the change in revenue
     per outlet?
tasks.predictQuestion: Which set of forms is right?

options.label: 1: a line over time; 2: horizontal bars sorted by size; 3: a scatter plot; 4: a waterfall
options.why: Each form encodes exactly what's being asked: a line for continuous change over time, bars for comparing magnitudes across categories, points for the relationship between two numeric quantities, a waterfall for how the parts contribute to a total change.

options.label: 1: bars by week; 2: a pie by region; 3: a line; 4: a table
options.why: Bars over a hundred weeks turn into a picket fence where the trend can't be read. A pie answers a question about shares of a whole, not "who lost the most." A line connects points that have no order between them. A table doesn't show contribution; the reader has to work it out by eye.

options.label: All four as bars: it's the most understandable form, people read it with no explanation
options.why: A form being understandable is no substitute for it fitting the question. Bars really are easy to read, but on a time series of a hundred weeks they hide the very thing the chart is built for: the shape of the change.

options.label: 1: a line; 2: vertical bars; 3: a scatter plot; 4: a pie
options.why: Three of the four are right; the error is in the last one. A pie shows shares of a whole, while the question is about contribution to a change; there are positive and negative parts, and they can't fit into a circle in principle.

hints: For each question, name the type of comparison: over time, across categories, between two numbers, or contribution to a total.
Horizontal bars beat vertical ones when the category names are long; you don't have to tilt them.
tasks.explain:
A chart isn't an illustration for the text, it's a way to answer a question faster than a table can. Hence the single rule for choosing one: state the question in a sentence first, then pick the form that encodes the answer.

Four basic types of comparison cover nearly everything an analyst needs. Change over time (a line): the eye reads slope as speed and breaks as events. Comparison across categories, bars sorted by size, and horizontal ones if the names are long. The relationship between two numeric quantities, a scatter plot, the only form where you see the relationship, its absence, and the outliers alike. Contribution of parts to a change in a total, a waterfall, invented for decomposition specifically.

The pie chart deserves its own word, because it's the default in every editor. Its legitimate territory is narrow: shares of a single whole, when the parts are few, differ markedly, and genuinely sum to a hundred percent. Everything else it does badly; people compare angles worse than lengths, and negative values don't fit into it at all. For the fourth question that disqualifies it immediately: losing outlets pulls down, revenue growth per outlet pushes up.

On sorting and orientation: bars sorted by size answer "who is biggest" instantly, while the same bars in alphabetical order force the reader to sort by eye. That's the cheapest edit in any deck and one of the most noticeable.

And on "a consistent look." What should be consistent is the styling: palette, fonts, axis labels, legend order. The form of the chart obeys the question, not the layout; identical charts for different questions aren't style, they're a refusal to answer.

tasks.title: The axis a conclusion starts from
tasks.brief: "Vitanor" grew 3.2% over the rolling year. Marketing draws it as bars with an axis not from zero: the last bar is three times the first.
tasks.goal: Decide when a cut axis lies.
tasks.predictQuestion: What is right?

options.label: Bars need an axis from zero; a line may be cut, visibly
options.why: A bar is read by length; cutting changes the ratio the eye sees. A line encodes slope and needs no zero, but a scale break is labelled.

options.label: Never cut an axis, anywhere
options.why: True for bars, harmful as a universal rule: temperature or an exchange rate drawn from zero is pointless, the swings become a straight line.

options.label: Any chart may be cut if an honest figure is printed
options.why: The reader believes the picture, not the caption: the shape is the conclusion they take away. "+3.2%" under bars three times apart reads as a technical detail.

options.label: In internal reports scale is free
options.why: Internal decisions cost money like external promises. "Fine for our own" ends in a budget set by a picture, not by the number.

figure.title: One series, two charts
head: Chart
What you see
rows: the last bar is three times the first
figure.note: The figure under the chart is the same in both: +3.2%.

hints: Ask what exactly the chart uses to encode magnitude: bar length or line slope.
Check the extreme case: what would a chart of the dollar exchange rate look like drawn from zero?
tasks.explain: The cut-axis dispute is settled by one question: how does the chart encode magnitude. A bar encodes by length, and "three times taller" reads as "three times more". Cutting the axis does not change the caption but changes the message. A line encodes by slope, so cutting is acceptable, but the scale break must be visible.

tasks.title: Twenty-nine slices of pie
tasks.brief: For the slide on portfolio concentration, a pie chart is proposed: 29 SKUs in the FMCG division, each with its share of revenue. The slide's question is "how dependent is the company on a few products."
tasks.goal: Choose the form that answers the slide's question.
tasks.scenario:
What's known about the FMCG portfolio:

  SKUs in total                 29
  the top 20% of SKUs give   36.3%
    of revenue
  to reach 80% of revenue you
    need            20 SKUs of 29

The slide's question: how dependent is
the company on a few products?
tasks.predictQuestion: Which form answers this question?

options.label: A Pareto chart: bars in descending order of share plus a cumulative-percentage line, which reads off directly how many SKUs you need to reach any threshold
options.why: The slide's question is about accumulation, not about individual shares. The cumulative curve answers it geometrically: you can see both that the top is modest and that reaching 80% means going all the way to the twentieth product.

options.label: A pie chart with 29 sectors: the most direct way to show shares of a whole
options.why: Twenty-nine sectors means most of them are thinner than their label. People can't compare angles that size, and a circle doesn't answer a question about accumulation at all: summing sectors by eye is impossible.

options.label: The top 8 products as bars, the rest as a single "other" row
options.why: A respectable form and the best one for many slides, but not for this question: rolling the rest into one "other" row hides exactly what's being asked about: the length of the tail. It would answer a different question, "who are our biggest products."

options.label: A table of all 29 SKUs with shares and a cumulative percentage
options.why: The data are all there, but the reader has to extract the conclusion himself by scanning two dozen rows. A table is good as an appendix to the slide or as a working tool, not as an answer to a question about the degree of concentration.

hints: Reread the slide's question: is it about individual shares, or about how many products it takes to reach a threshold?
Test each form against an action: can you answer "it takes N products to reach 80%" from it without doing arithmetic in your head?
tasks.explain:
The form is chosen to fit the question, and in this task the question is stated with unusual precision: not "what are the products' shares" but "how dependent are we on a few." That's a question about accumulation, and what answers it is a cumulative curve, not a set of shares.

A Pareto chart combines two encodings: descending bars show each product's contribution, the cumulative-percentage line shows how much has been gathered by each rank. The reader runs their eye from the threshold they care about to the curve and gets the answer without computing. On these data they'll see two things at once: the top is small (the top 20% of products give only 36.3%) and the tail is long (reaching 80% of revenue takes twenty products out of twenty-nine). The conclusion (concentration is moderate) matters more for an assortment decision than any individual share.

On a pie with two dozen sectors: the problem isn't aesthetics, it's that it doesn't answer. Even if a person could compare thin angles, they can't sum them by eye, and the question demands precisely a sum. The general rule: a circle is acceptable for three to five parts of one whole with markedly different shares, and almost always it can be replaced by a single stacked bar, where shares are compared by length.

The "top 8 and other" option is worth remembering as a good technique; it rescues most overloaded charts. But here it loses for the same reason it wins elsewhere: it deliberately collapses the tail, and the tail is what the question is about.

Separately, on the "20% of products give 80% of revenue" heuristic. People expect it by default, and when the data don't bear it out there's a strong temptation to bend the wording. Here the top 20% give 36.3%, and that's a meaningful result: the portfolio is spread more evenly than is usually assumed, the risk from delisting a single SKU is lower, but there will be no easy wins off a handful of hits either. Reading your own numbers matters more than checking them against someone else's rule.

tasks.title: Three revenues at one meeting
tasks.brief: At the annual committee three divisions quote three different 2025 revenues. Each is sure the others are wrong.
tasks.goal: Find what is broken and at which level.

figure.title: What the three divisions named
head: Division
Revenue, ¥
What it counts
figure.note: All three extracts are correct and reproducible.

tasks.predictQuestion: What is broken here?

options.label: The calculations are right; there is no fixed definition of revenue with an owner
options.why: Each figure is right in its own system: retail sold 51.5 million, we shipped 42.7, we will receive 39.1. There is no definition by which one of them is the right one.

options.label: Finance is right: revenue is money received
options.why: For a profit report, yes. But promos are planned on retail revenue, and warehouse load on shipments before discounts. Declaring one definition the only one just moves the dispute to the next meeting.

options.label: A technical problem: merge the sources into one warehouse
options.why: A warehouse does not choose between definitions: it stores all three and adds a fourth. A single mart follows an agreement on meaning, it does not replace it.

options.label: The analyst is to blame: reconcile before the committee
options.why: Reconciling before the meeting treats a symptom: a month later the same happens in another report. A one-off check creates no rule.

hints: Check each number for an error: is even one of them wrong?
Ask who in the company has the right to say "revenue is calculated like this", and where that's written down.
tasks.explain: A gap between figures almost never means someone calculated wrongly: everyone calculated something different correctly. Three numbers answer three questions: how much the shopper bought, how much we shipped and how much we will receive in cash. The fix is a metric definition with an owner and a place to record it, not a reconciliation.

tasks.title: The reference table rewrote last year
tasks.brief: In June outlet #1042 moved from "Prima" to "Ichiba" and the chain was replaced in the register. In July last year's report figures changed.
tasks.goal: Understand what happened to the history.

figure.title: Last year's report by chain
head: Chain
In January
In July
figure.note: Last year's sales did not change. One register attribute changed, and outlet #1042's sales for the whole year moved to the new chain.

tasks.predictQuestion: What is the defect?

options.label: The register keeps only the current state; the attribute needs validity dates
options.why: The report assigns the outlet's whole history to its current chain. Versioning fixes it: validity dates on the register row, joining by sale date.

options.label: No defect: a report reflects today's position
options.why: Currency matters for planning, not for a report on the past. If history silently changes, periods cannot be compared: any gap may be a register edit.

options.label: Recalculate and resend all past reports
options.why: That makes the problem systematic: every move rewrites the past again. Reports that decisions were based on cannot be changed retroactively.

options.label: Save finished reports as files
options.why: A file freezes one picture but cannot compute anything new by past rules: a new cut has nothing to reconcile against.

hints: Sales didn't change, so what changed is the thing they're joined to. What exactly?
Ask which question the report is asking: "how much did this chain sell back then" or "how much do the outlets that are in this chain today sell."
tasks.explain: The classic slowly changing dimension trap. Facts are immutable; the register they join to changes, and with it the whole history. Both answers are needed: "what did Prima sell last year" uses validity dates, "what does the chain look like today" the current value.

tasks.title: A request to send over an extract
tasks.brief: A consultant hired to optimize logistics writes in the work chat asking for an extract on the reps (full names, territory, outlet revenue, plan fulfillment): "to look at the data and get a picture." There is a contract with them, and the task was set by a manager.
tasks.goal: Choose what to do with a request like this.
tasks.scenario:
What's being asked for:

  rep's full name, team, territory,
  revenue of the outlets served over
  two years, monthly plan fulfillment

What's known:

  there is a contract with the consultant,
  the task is logistics optimization,
  the purpose of the extract isn't stated
  in the request, the chat is a shared one
  with about twenty people in it
tasks.predictQuestion: What do you do?

options.label: Clarify which question they're solving, hand over the minimum that serves it (by territory without names, say), and send it not through the shared chat but after clearing it with the data owner
options.why: Three actions close three different risks: clarifying the purpose cuts out unnecessary fields, de-identifying removes personal data where the task doesn't need it, and the sign-off and the transfer channel record who authorized it and where it went.

options.label: Send it: there's a contract, a manager set the task, the data are internal and aren't a trade secret
options.why: A contract answers "may I work with this person," not "do they need these fields." Names alongside plan fulfillment amount to an assessment of people, and logistics can be optimized on territories and volumes.

options.label: Refuse: extracts containing personal data are never shared externally under any circumstances
options.why: A flat refusal looks safe but halts work the company paid for. Governance is about handing over exactly what's needed and leaving a trail, not about handing over nothing.

options.label: Send it to the shared chat marked "confidential, do not forward"
options.why: A marking doesn't restrict access, it only records an intention. A file in a chat of twenty people has already spread: it will be downloaded, forwarded, and found by search a year from now, long after the consultant is gone.

hints: Split the question into three: which fields this task needs, who authorizes releasing them, and by what route they'll travel.
Ask whether the logistics task can be solved without knowing anyone's surname.
tasks.explain:
The answer to a request like this consists of three independent decisions, and they must not be conflated. First, the composition of the data: which fields are genuinely needed for the stated task. Second, the basis: who in the company owns these data and authorizes the transfer. Third, the channel: how exactly they'll travel and whether a trail remains.

On composition, the principle is minimization: hand over what the task can't be solved without, and nothing beyond it. Logistics optimization works with territories, outlets, volumes and distances; the reps' surnames aren't needed for it. Drop the names, replace them with a territory code, and the task is still fully solvable while the sensitivity of the extract falls by an order of magnitude. Plan fulfillment is data about the appraisal of specific people's work, and it most likely ended up in the request simply because it sat in the same table.

On the basis: a contract is a necessary condition, not a sufficient one. Authorization comes from the data owner, not from whoever is technically able to run the extract. For an analyst that's protection first of all for themselves: the decision to release wasn't theirs alone and it's on record.

On the channel: a shared chat isn't a data transfer channel. A file in it can't be recalled, restricted, or traced to see who downloaded it. The minimum standard is a link with access limited to a specific person and an expiry date; better still, access to a data mart instead of a file; access can be revoked, a file can't.

And on the tone of the reply. The clarifying question "which question exactly are you solving" isn't bureaucratic resistance, it's a normal professional response: it almost always shrinks the extract, and it often turns out that what was needed wasn't a list but two numbers. Refusing with no alternative and handing over without looking are two sides of one mistake: in both, the analyst didn't do the work, they dodged the decision.

tasks.title: Bad news about someone else's work
tasks.brief: Analysis of the "Milvara" promo for Thursday's committee. Trade marketing reported "2.5 times growth" all quarter; you work with them every week.
tasks.goal: Choose how to deliver bad news.
tasks.predictQuestion: What do you do with the analysis before Thursday?

options.label: Show them the numbers early, take the analysis to committee unchanged
options.why: Learning in public turns the talk into defending a reputation. A heads-up does not soften the finding; it removes the surprise.

options.label: Take it as is with no warning: they would prepare objections
options.why: Substantive objections are useful. The risk is different: told in public, a person defends themselves and the debate slides to who is to blame.

options.label: Soften: drop the comparison with trade marketing's report
options.why: Drop the comparison and you drop the finding: the repeat decision would use a figure twice the real return.

options.label: Hand them the analysis: let them decide what to bring
options.why: The committee asked, not them: the result goes back to whoever asked. Handing it over makes them editor of their own assessment.

hints: For each option, picture the conversation at the committee: will it be about how the promo worked, or about who got it wrong?
One option protects the relationship at the cost of the conclusion. Check what is left of the analysis once the comparison is gone.
tasks.explain: "No surprises": a person whose work gets bad news hears it from you, before the audience. It is not politeness: publicly surprised, they cannot respond on substance, the talk turns to reputation and the decision is not made. A heads-up gives no veto, it gives time to check.

tasks.title: Three positions and fifteen minutes
tasks.brief: Committee on the "Nettora" brand: revenue −49%, 46 of 79 outlets stopped selling. The budget decision is today and you have 15 minutes.
tasks.goal: Understand what the dispute is made of.

figure.title: Three voices and what you know
head: Who
Says
rows: The brand drags us down, cut support
The numbers are wrong, the outlets are there
The dashboard shows 60 active outlets, not 33
46 outlets had no brand sales this quarter; BI counts an outlet active for a year after its last shipment

tasks.predictQuestion: Where do you start?

options.label: Split it into three: definition, fact, decision; price each option for the third
options.why: Only two voices are about numbers. The definition and the list of 46 close at once; whether to cut is a choice, and your part is the price of each option.

options.label: Back the finance director: the conclusion matches yours
options.why: Your analysis explains the drop but does not say cut: the same numbers support winning back the 46. Joining a side costs you independence.

options.label: Postpone a week until the three sources are reconciled
options.why: The BI gap closes with one sentence and you hold the list. A week buys a delay; the budget is decided today, without you.

options.label: Prove your number is right: BI counts shipments
options.why: Being right on method answers none of the three: BI counts a different metric, and finance is not talking about a number.

hints: For each remark ask: is this a claim about a fact, about a definition, or about what to do?
One of the three positions cannot be checked against data at all, which does not make it wrong.
tasks.explain: A table dispute is rarely uniform: sort it by type of disagreement first. A disagreement about fact closes with a checkable claim ("here are 46 outlets, name any"), one about definition with one sentence, one about a decision with the price of each option, not by winning.

tasks.title: A metric someone else's report rests on
tasks.brief: You have been at the company three months. The "average revenue per outlet" metric shows +22% while "Nettora" revenue halved: small outlets left.
tasks.goal: Choose how to challenge someone else's metric.

figure.title: Average revenue per outlet, Nettora
head: Item
Value
figure.note: The rest is a mix effect. The metric has been in the report for three years, a bonus depends on it, and its owner heads commercial analytics.

tasks.predictQuestion: How do you challenge it?

options.label: One to one with the owner, on a concrete case; propose a second metric beside it
options.why: Argue with the decision the metric misleads, not with the metric: +22% while revenue halves is a case the owner will see. Adding rather than cancelling keeps three years of history.

options.label: Break it down in a group mailing with this example
options.why: A public breakdown of someone's metric reads as an accusation, and they will discuss you, not the average. The owner cannot agree without losing face.

options.label: Nothing: it is not yours, you have been here three months
options.why: Tenure is no argument: the signal is false or it is not. Staying silent makes you answerable for conclusions from a metric you think wrong, and each quarter it is harder to challenge.

options.label: Calculate your own way in your own reports
options.why: Two figures for one thing appear with no explanation, and the talk about the signal becomes a dispute over who calculates correctly. A metric changes by agreement, with a date.

hints: Ask which decision is made on this metric and where exactly that decision goes wrong: what you challenge is the decision, not the number.
One option is right on the substance but chosen so that nobody can agree with it without losing face.
tasks.explain: A metric is challenged by a case, not by the claim "it is wrong": that claim has to be defended, and the person defends, not the metric. +22% average revenue per outlet while brand revenue halves is an ideal case: it checks in minutes and does not ask anyone to take your word.

tasks.title: A question the data cannot answer
tasks.brief: The sales director wants one figure for the board: how much revenue "Nettora" lost by being absent from the shelf in 46 outlets. Data on sales that never happened exists nowhere.
tasks.goal: Answer without inventing a number.

figure.title: What exists and what does not
head: What
Details
rows: 46 outlets with no sales; their 2024 revenue; the trend of comparable outlets that stayed (+9.7%)
what they would have bought in those outlets had the product been on the shelf

tasks.predictQuestion: What do you tell the sales director?

options.label: Estimate from the 46 outlets' past revenue with a stated assumption; say it is an upper bound
options.why: The board needs an order of magnitude for the negotiation budget. An estimate with its method written beside it gives that and stays honest: the number is derived, not measured.

options.label: Say there is no such data: any number is invented
options.why: Formally true and useless: the board will name a figure anyway, without assumptions. "No data" answers "is there data", not "is it worth going back".

options.label: Give a number from past revenue with no caveats
options.why: The assumption is obvious to you today, but a month later the number is quoted from the slide as a measured loss. An assumption not written beside the number does not exist.

options.label: Average brand revenue per outlet times 46
options.why: The departed outlets are smaller than those that stayed (24,738 ¥ against 29,810 ¥), so the brand average overstates the loss. Simplicity is no reason to use a wrong base.

hints: Separate what is physically absent from the data from what can be estimated out of what you do have, with one named assumption.
For each option, check what actually lands on the board's slide and how it will be read a month later without you.
tasks.explain: There are three answers, not two: cannot be measured, say so; can be estimated, estimate; write the assumption beside the number, do not say it aloud. The base is the past revenue of exactly these 46 outlets, not the brand average. The adjustment is the trend of comparable outlets, and the figure is called an upper-bound estimate.

tasks.title: Asked to lead with a different number
tasks.brief: A slide for the board: "Nettora" revenue −49%, cause: 46 outlets left. The manager asks for +22% per outlet in the headline: "the talk goes calmer".
tasks.goal: Answer a request that changes the conclusion.

figure.title: Both figures from one analysis
head: Measure
Value
figure.note: The +22% comes from 46 outlets leaving: they were smaller than those that stayed, so the average rose by itself. Request: put +22% in the headline and mention the decline if asked.

tasks.predictQuestion: What do you do with the slide?

options.label: The headline answers the board's question; +22% beside it as part of the explanation
options.why: The headline answers the board's question. +22% explains the mechanics of the decline but should not come first; a line on the mix effect stops it being read as success.

options.label: Do as asked: the headline is the manager's call
options.why: Both numbers are right, but the board will complete the conclusion "the brand is growing". A silent swap that changes the conclusion is the same distortion as omission: honest numbers, false picture.

options.label: Refuse to make the slide
options.why: The request is not absurd: a slide with only −49% starts a panic. Refusing turns a dispute about form into a conflict, and someone else makes the slide without your caveats.

options.label: Put both figures in the headline with no link explained
options.why: Two opposite figures with no explanation shift the work: each reader picks the convenient one and the talk becomes a dispute over which is real. Linking them is your part.

hints: Ask what question the board was convened for, and whether the figure you are asked to lead with answers it.
One option formally shows everything and communicates nothing.
tasks.explain: Tell pressure on form from pressure on conclusion. Form (order, emphasis, tone) is negotiable: the manager knows the audience and the cost of panic better. The conclusion the reader leaves with is not. One-sentence test: if after the edit the reader would understand the brand differently, it is an edit of the conclusion.

tasks.title: An error in a report already sent
tasks.brief: After the analysis went out you find an error: the channel table lost e-commerce. The conclusion holds, but negotiations began with the wrong channel.
tasks.goal: Choose how to correct it.

figure.title: What the report said and what is true
head: Channel
In the report
In fact
figure.note: Forty people read the report; negotiations with chains began yesterday. The conclusion about 46 outlets does not change.

tasks.predictQuestion: How do you correct it?

options.label: Write at once to those whose decision rests on the table; a short fix to the rest after
options.why: Negotiations run today, so speed beats completeness. A line like "conclusion unchanged, priority changed" lets a reader see in ten seconds whether the fix touches their actions.

options.label: Quietly replace the table in the file and dashboard
options.why: People act on the version they saw, and a fixed file will not reach them. A silent fix turns one error into two: which version to trust?

options.label: A detailed apology to all forty
options.why: Those negotiating need ten seconds to see whether to change the plan; a confession pushes the point to the end. Root cause matters, but separately and later.

options.label: Fix it in the next weekly report
options.why: A week is a week of negotiating with a channel worth 17% of revenue instead of 80%. The cost of silence is the work of people acting on your figure.

hints: Ask whose action tomorrow changes because of this correction. That is where the recipient list starts.
One option makes the correction invisible to exactly the people already acting on the old version.
tasks.explain: Correcting an error already sent has an order, and it is not about apologies. First: who is acting on this figure; write to them at once, since every hour of work on the wrong priority is paid for. Second: what is wrong, in which direction and by how much. Everyone else gets a short fix after. Root causes are reviewed separately and later.

tasks.title: Three months that add nothing
tasks.brief: At the annual accuracy review the planner shows the demand forecast error and puts the error of a free benchmark next to it: «we will sell what we sold last month». Production plans line loading three months ahead.
tasks.goal: Work out what this table implies for the planning cycle.
tasks.scenario:
Forecast error, % of yearly volume:

horizon     forecast   calendar
1 month        15%        33%
2 months       27%        34%
3 months       31%        34%

Calendar means «we will sell what
we sold last month».
Production plans three months ahead.
tasks.predictQuestion: What does this mean for the planning cycle?

options.label: At the horizon the forecast exists for, it barely differs from a free benchmark: say that out loud and find the cause first, and improve the model after
options.why: One month ahead the forecast earns its keep: 15% against 33%. At three months the advantage is three points, and that is exactly the horizon production needs. The conversation starts with admitting that the far horizon currently rides on the calendar, not with a new model.

options.label: The forecast is bad: 31% error is not a forecast, the model has to be replaced
options.why: Bad compared to what? The calendar gives 34% at the same horizon, so «bad» here is a property of the problem rather than of the model. An absolute error with no benchmark says nothing: 31% is a disaster on one product and a good result on another.

options.label: Extend the forecast horizon to six months so that production can plan more calmly
options.why: Accuracy falls with the horizon, so the sixth month will be worse than the third. Calm comes from an honest statement of what can be trusted at each horizon, not from the length of the forecast.

options.label: If the calendar is no worse, the planner is not needed: take the benchmark and close the cycle
options.why: At the near horizon the forecast is twice as accurate as the calendar, and procurement and shipments live on that horizon. Dropping the forecast would spend that half to save on the far one.

hints: Compare the two columns row by row rather than as a whole: the distance between them matters more than either number.
Ask at which horizon the decision that the forecast exists for is actually taken.
tasks.explain: The first question to ask of any forecast is not «how accurate is it» but «is it better than what costs nothing». The free benchmark here is the simplest one: repeat last month. One month ahead the forecast beats it twice over, and that is its legitimate value; at three months the gap is three points, and the line loading decision is taken exactly there. The distance between forecast and benchmark is called forecast value added, and it is measured at each horizon separately, because a single yearly figure hides the very thing worth seeing. What to do about it is not something the data can say, and that is fine: there are usually two moves, shorten the horizon of firm commitments, or feed the far forecast what people know about the future and the series does not, such as the promo plan, a new retailer, a competitor leaving. One caveat about the benchmark itself: repeating last month works badly for a seasonal product, where the fairer comparison is the same month a year ago. Pick the benchmark in advance and name it out loud, or the argument about the value of forecasting turns into an argument about what to compare it with.

tasks.title: Eight run low, one runs high
tasks.brief: The annual accuracy review carries forecast bias for every brand: how far above or below actuals the forecast sits on average. The planner says it is just spread.
tasks.goal: Work out what this picture says first of all.
tasks.scenario:
Forecast bias for the year, three month
horizon, % of actuals
(plus means overshot):

  Nettora      +11%
  Rhinolar      -6%
  Vitanor       -7%
  Fruvia        -8%
  Milvara       -8%
  Pyrexan      -10%
  Gastrivo     -11%
  Krosti       -14%
  Aqualis      -15%

Nettora has been falling for two years.
tasks.predictQuestion: What does this picture say first of all?

options.label: It is about the process rather than the model: eight brands out of nine run low, and a one sided lean comes from people and rules, not from chance
options.why: Random error would scatter pluses and minuses. Eight minuses in a row mean the numbers are steadily pushed one way, usually in the sign off meeting, where a lower forecast is safer for the plan and the bonus. A lean like that can be measured and subtracted as a correction, which is cheaper than any new model.

options.label: «Nettora» is forecast better than the others: it holds the only plus in the column
options.why: The sign says nothing about accuracy. On a falling brand the forecast runs high because a return to the old level is built into it every month, and the error there is in fact the worst on the list. Bias and accuracy are two different quantities.

options.label: The model errs systematically and has to be retrained on fresh data
options.why: A model that errs one way on eight brands at once is rare; a lean like that usually comes from manual edits and sign off rules layered on top of the calculation. Retraining leaves the cause untouched, and a quarter later the picture returns.

options.label: Nothing: a bias within fifteen percent is normal for demand forecasting
options.why: What is normal is the spread, not its one sidedness. Fifteen percent either way is ordinary life; fifteen percent always in the same direction means somebody or something is holding the numbers down.

hints: Look at the signs rather than the sizes: how many brands went down and how many went up.
Ask what this column would look like if the error were random.
tasks.explain: Bias answers the question «which way», and the answer here is one sided: eight brands out of nine are forecast below actuals. Chance does not look like that, so somebody is moving the numbers, and it usually happens after the model rather than inside it: a lower demand forecast is safer for the sales plan that bonuses are paid on, and easier in the conversation with production. Hence the practical conclusion: a steady lean is the cheapest part of the error, subtracted as a correction for an improvement with no new model at all, while the random part is far harder to reduce. The ninth row matters more than the eight, though. On the falling brand the lean runs the other way, because a return to the old level is built into the forecast every month, and that is no longer a general rule but the specific expectation of specific people. So the rule for reading the table: show bias and accuracy side by side and never one in place of the other. Bias speaks about the process and the people, error speaks about how predictable the task is at all.

tasks.title: The order of checks before you send
tasks.brief: The number 41,726,300 ¥ is ready and the meeting is in 40 minutes. The order of checks is not free: one mistake voids the rest.
tasks.goal: Put the five pre-send checks in order.
tasks.orderQuestion: In what order do you run them?

items.label: Did you compute what was asked: metric, period, breakdown
items.why: First: a wrong metric voids every other check, and the recipient notices it, not you.

items.label: The period is closed, no late data
items.why: Second: reconciling a quarter whose last days have not arrived means hunting for a gap that does not exist.

items.label: Reconcile the total with an independent source
items.why: Third: it catches an error in the calculation itself, a lost join or duplicates. Earlier is impossible, later is pointless.

items.label: Look at the breakdown: blanks, outliers, zeros
items.why: Fourth: a total can match while errors cancel out. The breakdown catches them, but only on a confirmed total.

items.label: Write the metric definition next to the number
items.why: Last: this is insurance, not a check. A definition mismatch surfaces in the email, not at the meeting.

hints: One of these checks can void any of the other four, however long you spent on them. Start there.
There is a dependency between reconciling against a source and looking at the breakdown: one of them dissects the result of the other, and it does not work the other way round.
The final item is the only one that checks nothing in your data at all. It is about what happens after you press send.
tasks.explain: Do first what can void the rest: a wrong metric definition ruins any work after it. Then by shrinking radius: complete data, reconciliation, breakdown. The last step checks nothing in the data; it insures against a definition mismatch.

tasks.title: A churn report: where to start
tasks.brief: The sales director asks for a "churn report by Thursday". "Churn" is not defined and the decision is not named.
tasks.goal: Put the framing steps in order.
tasks.orderQuestion: In what order do you turn the request into a brief?

items.label: Ask which decision the result feeds and who makes it
items.why: First: everything else follows from the decision. "Keep customers" and "explain the drop" are different reports from the same data.

items.label: Turn the request into a question with a checkable answer
items.why: Second: the decision names an area, the question narrows it to one answer. "Calculated correctly" only exists relative to a question.

items.label: Choose the metric and write down its definition
items.why: Third: the metric follows from the question. "Churn" can be counted five ways, and each gives its own conclusion.

items.label: Check the data exists for the needed period
items.why: Fourth, before building: if history is short, the metric or question changes. Now that costs ten minutes, later the whole deadline.

items.label: Confirm the done criterion and deadline in writing
items.why: Last: a written done criterion stops the endless "can you add one more cut" and makes Thursday a promise.

hints: One of the steps gives all the others their content, and without it each of them comes down to a coin toss.
Between "which metric" and "does the data exist" there is a direction: one of them can cancel the other, and only one way round.
The last step finds out nothing about the subject. It is about how the work ends.
tasks.explain: Framing is a chain: the decision sets the question, the question the metric, the metric the data needs, and only then the done criterion. A metric chosen before the question is an answer invented before the task. If the decision is not named, it is too early to start.

tasks.title: A definition two people will agree on
tasks.brief: Two teams have argued for a second month about how to calculate average sale price. You need to pin down the definition.
tasks.goal: Put the definition steps in order.
tasks.orderQuestion: In what order do you build a metric definition?

items.label: Find out whether an approved definition already exists
items.why: First: this step can cancel the rest. Your own definition beside an existing one is a second truth, and a two-team dispute becomes three-way.

items.label: Name the event counted and the date field
items.why: Second: this is the subject of the definition. Until it says shipments or shelf sales, there is nothing to refine; the date field follows from the event.

items.label: List exclusions: returns, internal turnover
items.why: Third: you can only exclude from a named set, otherwise it is unclear whether you subtract from sales, shipments or orders.

items.label: State units, currency and rounding
items.why: Fourth: this is the shape of the answer. It removes everyday gaps like roubles per unit versus thousands per pack.

items.label: Agree with the owner and put it next to the number
items.why: Last: agreeing an unfinished definition is agreeing on nothing. Next to the number, because nobody reads a definition they have to go find.

hints: One of the steps can end the work in the first minute. It is also the least pleasant one, because it voids the definition you had already drafted.
Ask what the exclusions are subtracted from. The answer tells you which item has to come earlier.
The last two items do not narrow the subject: one sets the form, the other puts the definition into circulation.
tasks.explain: A definition is built from subject to refinements: you can only exclude from what is named. The first step stands apart: it decides whether the work is needed at all, since a duplicate definition is worse than none. One test: two people read it and get the same number.

tasks.title: Five links and five different numbers
tasks.brief: A pack is counted at every link between factory and shopper, and the numbers differ: a warehouse sits between the links.
tasks.goal: Put the links in the order the goods move.
tasks.orderQuestion: In what order does the product pass the links?

items.label: Manufacturer ships to distributor: sell-in
items.why: First: without this shipment there is no product in the chain. It is the most reliable number, which is why it is so often mistaken for sales.

items.label: Distributor warehouse: channel stock
items.why: Second: the warehouse explains the main gap: sell-in has happened, sell-out has not. Forgetting it means mistaking overstock for demand.

items.label: Distributor ships to the outlet
items.why: Third: you can ship to an outlet only what is in the warehouse. From here data is the partner's: late and incomplete.

items.label: Outlet puts the product on the shelf
items.why: Fourth, and this link may never happen: stock can sit in a back room all season. The gap is measured by audit.

items.label: Shopper takes the pack off the shelf: sell-out
items.why: Last: the only real demand is here. The rest is goods moving through a pipe.

hints: Follow the pack itself rather than the money: in this chain the money travels the other way.
One of the links is not movement but standing still. It is what explains why two neighbouring numbers disagree.
One link can fail to happen even though the previous one did. It is the second to last.
tasks.explain: The chain also sets the order of trust in the numbers: the closer to the shopper, the more it says about demand and the worse the data. The industry's main mistake is calling sell-in "sales" because it is at hand. Any claim about demand names the link it was measured at.

tasks.title: From order to cash: five marks
tasks.brief: Order #4417 for 4,700,000 ¥ has shipped, no cash on the account. The director asks why sales are closed.
tasks.goal: Put the order-to-cash marks in order.
tasks.orderQuestion: In what order do they occur?

items.label: Customer places the order: order date
items.why: First: the cycle starts with the customer's commitment. It is the least reliable mark: an order can be cancelled, so planning on it is planning on intent.

items.label: Order confirmed, stock reserved
items.why: Second: a reservation is only possible against an existing order. It explains why free stock is lower than physical stock.

items.label: Goods shipped: shipment date
items.why: Third: revenue is recognised here. Not at the order, which is not fulfilled, and not at payment, which is for goods already delivered.

items.label: Invoice issued: receivable appears
items.why: Fourth: you cannot invoice what has not shipped. The amount then lives twice, in revenue and in receivables: two sides of one fact.

items.label: Cash arrives: receivable closes
items.why: Last: payment closes the invoice. The length of the delay between the third mark and this one is the answer to the director.

hints: Two marks belong to the goods, two belong to the money, and one moves nothing at all.
Find the mark where revenue is recognised. It is neither the first nor the last, and it is the most common place to get this wrong.
You cannot invoice for something the customer has not received yet.
tasks.explain: Order-to-cash is a list of dates the analyst chooses between: March gives one figure by order date, another by shipment, a third by payment, and all are valid. A report must name the mark it is built on. The gap between sales and cash is the payment delay, not a defect.

tasks.title: The monthly planning cycle
tasks.brief: You run the S&OP cycle. At the last meeting they argued about the plan before the actuals were closed and left with nothing.
tasks.goal: Put the monthly cycle steps in order.
tasks.orderQuestion: In what order do they go?

items.label: Close last month's actuals, update the history
items.why: First: everything rests on history. A forecast on an unclosed month is understated and will change by itself, with no decision.

items.label: Compute a statistical forecast with no manual edits
items.why: Second: you need a baseline for the adjustments. Without it you cannot tell data from expectations or judge the quality of the work.

items.label: Collect commercial adjustments: promos, listings, a lost customer
items.why: Third: an adjustment is an adjustment to something. With a baseline each one has a size and a reason, and next month you can see if it came true.

items.label: Check feasibility: capacity, materials, warehouse
items.why: Fourth: supply answers demand that is already fixed. Otherwise you get a plan of what is convenient to produce.

items.label: Agree one plan as a commitment
items.why: Last: the decision is made over the combined number. The agreed plan becomes the baseline for next month's actuals.

hints: One step produces a number, another edits it, a third checks whether that can be delivered. What do all three start from?
Ask why a machine should forecast at all if people are going to correct it anyway. The answer places both steps.
Supply answers a question. So the question has to be asked earlier.
tasks.explain: Demand and the ability to meet it are discussed separately and in this order, or the forecast quietly turns into a production plan. The statistical baseline keeps people's adjustments visible: the gap to the agreed plan is the commercial team's contribution (forecast value added).

tasks.title: What to do before subtracting one period from another
tasks.brief: On the dashboard March is below February and you owe an explanation by lunch. A difference is only readable after preparation.
tasks.goal: Put the comparison prep steps in order.
tasks.orderQuestion: In what order do you do them?

items.label: Choose the base: last month or a year ago
items.why: First: all the work runs against the base. "Down" without a base means nothing: a drop versus February is growth versus last March.

items.label: Make periods comparable: days, perimeter
items.why: Second: you can only align a chosen pair. Calendar and perimeter move the difference without changing demand or price.

items.label: Remove one-offs: a promo, a big single shipment
items.why: Third: a one-off is subtracted in units of the comparable pair. Otherwise you subtract one inaccuracy from another.

items.label: Read the remainder: seasonality or real change
items.why: Fourth: until now the remainder holds everything at once. Only now does "seasonality or not" make sense.

items.label: Check the conclusion on a neighbouring cut
items.why: Last: you can only check a finished conclusion. The step catches an explanation true for one row and false for the next.

hints: The first step computes nothing and corrects nothing. It only names what we compare against, and without it the other four have no subject.
Calendar and perimeter sit in one item for a reason: both remove a gap that was never in demand.
One of the steps does not prepare the comparison but tests a conclusion that already exists. It is last.
tasks.explain: A difference is the cheapest operation and the costliest source of false conclusions, because it always shows something. First make the pair comparable, then subtract one-offs, then name the remainder. A conclusion resting on one report row is usually coincidence.

tasks.title: Promotion payback: the order of counting
tasks.brief: The agency reports the promotion worked: −25% on "Aqualis", two weeks, sales are up. Only the promo period was calculated.
tasks.goal: Put the promo return steps in order.
tasks.orderQuestion: In what order do you calculate it?

items.label: Define the base: sales without the promo
items.why: First: lift is the difference from the base, not sales during the promo. Without a base the number says "how much sold", not "what the promo gave".

items.label: Calculate lift against the base
items.why: Second: you can only subtract from a defined base. It is the most inflated figure: the next steps only reduce it.

items.label: Look at the weeks after: the dip
items.why: Third: part of the lift is borrowed from the coming weeks, because shoppers stocked up. The dip is subtracted from lift.

items.label: Check neighbouring SKUs: cannibalisation
items.why: Fourth: cannibalisation is subtracted from lift net of the dip. This step is skipped most often, since it means looking beyond the promo.

items.label: Add up the economics: discount versus gain
items.why: Last: money is counted on the final volume. A promo with a gain in units often turns out loss-making here.

hints: The first two steps give you the largest number you are going to get. After that it only shrinks.
Two corrections reduce the lift for different reasons: one takes volume from the future, the other from the neighbour on the shelf.
One step converts units into money and changes the conclusion entirely. It cannot come before the units are final.
tasks.explain: Evaluating a promo is a chain of subtractions from one optimistic number, and each adjustment is calculated from the previous result. A report with only lift answers the wrong question. Base and cannibalisation are estimates; an honest report names how they were obtained.

tasks.title: A fall: in what order to take it apart
tasks.brief: March revenue is 18% below February, meeting at 15:00. Working top-down ends with an address; guessing ends with a plausible story.
tasks.goal: Put the drop-analysis steps in order.
tasks.orderQuestion: In what order do you work through it?

items.label: Confirm the drop is real: extract, lookup, filter
items.why: First: a good share of such stories end here. An extract artefact sliced by cuts looks like analysis but explains a load failure.

items.label: Split into volume and price
items.why: Second: a fork. Fewer units is a question for demand and shelf, lower price for discounts and mix; the two branches share almost no steps.

items.label: Find the cut with the biggest contribution: channel, brand, region
items.why: Third: you choose a cut knowing whether you are looking for volume or price. Slicing by every cut at once gives a table that implies nothing.

items.label: Get down to the customer or SKU
items.why: Fourth: narrowing continues until the number belongs to something you can act on. "The south fell" when two outlets of one chain fell is too early.

items.label: Name the owner and what they can do
items.why: Last: an analysis ending in a number, not a person, changes nothing. This step turns the result into someone else's task.

hints: One step can end the whole investigation in the first ten minutes, and it belongs before any breakdown at all.
Between "volume or price" and the choice of dimension there is a direction: one of them decides which dimensions are worth looking at.
The last step is not about data at all.
tasks.explain: The analysis runs top-down and each narrowing rests on the previous one. The first step decides whether there is anything to discuss, and it is skipped most when time is short. "Volume or price" comes before cuts because it decides which cuts are informative. It ends with an address.

tasks.title: The order of arguments about a cause
tasks.brief: At a meeting they said: "we launched the mailing, sales rose, so the mailing works". The checks run from cheap to decisive.
tasks.goal: Put the checks of a causal claim in order.
tasks.orderQuestion: In what order do you run them?

items.label: The link exists in the data, not in the retelling
items.why: First: every other check tests a link that must exist. It is the cheapest and often ends the talk: the story rests on two memorable months.

items.label: Cause comes before effect
items.why: Second: it cheaply kills a whole class of wrong claims. A mailing goes to active buyers, so the growth comes before it.

items.label: Look for a common cause of both quantities
items.why: Third: a common cause explains a real, correctly directed link. Season or a competitor promo moves both quantities.

items.label: Find a comparison: similar customers without the mailing
items.why: Fourth: a control group costs the most and is built for the claim that survived. It turns an explanation into proof.

items.label: Name the observation that would refute the conclusion
items.why: Last: it is stated about a finished conclusion. A claim nothing can refute is a belief, not a conclusion.

hints: The first two tests run on data you already have open. They are cheap, which is why they come first.
A common cause explains an association that exists and points the right way. So both properties have to be established before it.
One of the tests needs data you have not collected yet, and it is also the strongest one.
tasks.explain: Checks rise in cost: cheap ones weed out claims not worth building a control group for. The comparison is strongest, since it alone answers what would have happened without the intervention, which is what "affected" means. If you cannot name a refuting observation, the conclusion was usually never tested.

tasks.title: Five blocks and a shrinking audience
tasks.brief: A quarter-results email: four paragraphs, conclusion in the last. The director reads 10 seconds, the deputy half, a peer analyst opens the appendix.
tasks.goal: Order the blocks by shrinking audience.
tasks.orderQuestion: How do you structure the email?

items.label: One-sentence conclusion: what happened and what to do
items.why: First: everyone reads it. A conclusion sentence forces you to have one conclusion rather than four observations, and half the work on the email goes into it.

items.label: The one number the conclusion rests on
items.why: Second: the claim needs support at once, or it reads as opinion. One number, not a table: the reader is deciding whether to believe.

items.label: The cut that explains the number
items.why: Third: it unpacks the support for whoever wants to check. The first block you can skip without losing the point.

items.label: Method and caveats
items.why: Fourth: one reader in ten needs it, the one who will argue. Earlier, it buries the conclusion under conditions.

items.label: Appendix: tables, extracts, queries
items.why: Last: the appendix exists so the work can be repeated, not read. One reader, sometimes you yourself in six months.

hints: Ask not "what is logical to tell first" but "how many people will read as far as this".
The first two blocks are mandatory, the other three can be abandoned at any point without losing the main thing.
Caveats about method are needed by whoever argues. There are fewer of those than of people who simply read.
tasks.explain: The email is built by shrinking audience, the reverse of how the work went: you went from data to conclusion, the reader goes from conclusion to data. The first place is the most valuable, give it to the main claim. Test: cover everything but the first two lines and ask if that is enough to decide.

tasks.title: Annual report by month
tasks.brief: The report goes to the director in 10 minutes. Distributor sales by month for 2025.
tasks.goal: Mark everything that must not be sent.
tasks.orderQuestion: What must not be sent here?

spotMutate.why: A year has {expected} months, but the footer says "Rows: {rows}". A month dropped out, so the total is understated even though it looks plausible. The director will ask where the month went.

spotDecoys.why: September is the highest month, but high does not mean wrong. Compare it with last September: it was {n} thousand yen then, also well above the neighbouring months.

hints: How many rows should an annual report by month have?
Compare the counter in the footer with the number of months in a year.
tasks.explain: A missing period is the quietest kind of error: the query does not break, no value is distorted, and the total looks reasonable. There is only one way to catch it: before sending, you say how many rows you expect and compare with the counter. A mismatch means either a filter mistake or a hole in the data, and it has to be sorted out before sending. A high month proves nothing by itself: it is checked against the same month of last year.

tasks.title: Regions for December
tasks.brief: The report goes to the director in 10 minutes. Distributor sales by region for December 2025.
tasks.goal: Mark everything that must not be sent.
tasks.orderQuestion: What must not be sent here?

spotMutate.why: One region sold {value} thousand yen in a single month, while the whole company sold {n} thousand yen in a whole year. That cannot be: it is a sign of breakage, not an outlier. Rows may have multiplied in a join, or units may be mixed up. The director will ask where the figure comes from.

spotDecoys.why: Osaka is the smallest row, but small does not mean wrong: it is the smallest region over the whole year too, just {n} thousand yen.

hints: Compare each figure not with its neighbours but with the scale of the whole business.
Think about whether one region can sell more in a month than the whole company in a year.
tasks.explain: The order of magnitude check is the cheapest: it needs neither a recalculation nor access to the source, only knowing what units the business lives in. An analyst who remembers the company annual revenue notices an impossible figure in a fraction of a second. A rule without exceptions: a figure you cannot explain is not sent, with or without a caveat. A small figure alone is not a reason to worry either: check whether the size of the region explains it.

tasks.title: Regions for the year
tasks.brief: The report goes to the director in 10 minutes. Distributor sales by region for 2025.
tasks.goal: Mark everything that must not be sent.
tasks.orderQuestion: What must not be sent here?

spotMutate.why: The region appears in the list twice. This happens when a join finds two records for a region and rows multiply. The director will ask why there are two identical rows.

The rows add up to {sum}, but the footer "Total" says {total}: a difference of {delta} thousand yen. A total is always recalculated separately from the rows, and it must match. The director will add it up as soon as a figure looks odd.

spotDecoys.why: Fukuoka is the largest row, and that is correct: it has {n} distributors, more than most regions. High does not mean wrong.

hints: There are two defects. One is visible in the list, the other only after adding up.
Add the rows up, even roughly, and compare with the total.
tasks.explain: A report can hold more than one error, and the second often hides behind the first. A duplicated row shows to the eye, a total that differs from the sum of the rows only after adding up. That is why the check goes down a list: the counter, the order of magnitude, the sum. Stopping at the first error found means sending the second. And the reverse: a correct large row is not a defect, the data explains it.

tasks.title: Beverages by month
tasks.brief: The report goes to the director in 10 minutes. Distributor sales of beverages by month for 2025.
tasks.goal: Mark everything that must not be sent.
tasks.orderQuestion: What must not be sent here?

spotDecoys.why: June is higher than its neighbours, but beverages grow towards summer: last June was {n} thousand yen against {m} thousand yen in May. That is the season, not an error.
November is clearly below its neighbours, but it was weak a year ago too: {n} thousand yen then. Low does not mean wrong.

hints: Check the row counter, the order of magnitude and the total. Does everything add up?
Not every unusual number is an error: compare with the same month of last year.
tasks.explain: The skill of checking includes the skill of stopping when the check found nothing. A seasonal peak and a seasonal trough are not errors: they are compared with the same month of last year, not with the neighbours. Every extra mark is a question from the director and lost time, and holding back a correct report costs almost as much as sending a wrong one. Treat the check as finished when the counter, the scale and the total agree.
